newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa plans defence acquisitions to 2015.
newsitem.headline: South Africa plans defence acquisitions to 2015.

text.p: South Africa's defence force is continuing to plan ship, aircraft and tank purchases despite delays in a policy review intended to set the agenda for weapons acquisitions to 2015, officials said on Wednesday.

Defence Secretary Pierre Steyn, the senior civilian official in Defence Minister Joe Modise's staff, gave parliament's powerful standing committee on defence a document on procurement plans into the next century.
The package included details of a stalled 1.69 billion rand programme to buy four naval corvettes and referred to plans to replace the country's three aged French submarines.
Among 145 projects referred to during an open meeting with the committee, Steyn and officials revealed procurement projects in the pipeline including:
- A 1.35 billion rand plan ending in fiscal 2004/5 to buy 61 all-weather operational and training helicopters;
- A 3.38 billion rand project to buy 94 main battle tanks to replace the existing Olifant tanks by 2009;
- A programme to acquire as yet unidentified light fighter aircraft between 2009 and 2015;
- A plan referred to as "Project Impose" to buy 13 of the South African arms industry's own Rooivalk helicopter gunships;
- The purchase of 3,151 general purpose mine-protected infantry vehicles of a design still to be identified by fiscal 2010/11 at a cost of 765 million rand;
- The purchase of 242 local Rooikat armoured vehicles.

Under fire from African National Congress legislators for anticipating the outcome of a post-apartheid defence review, Steyn said that though money was being spent on all the projects, most could be stopped.
The defence review, originally scheduled to have been completed by now, is unlikely to be published before the 1997/98 budget is presented in March.
The review will resolve as yet unsettled questions about the level and type of defence capability South Africa plans to maintain.
There is strong pressure within the ruling ANC to cut dramatically defence spending in favour of social projects neglected under white rule.

Defence committee chairman Tony Yengeni, a veteran of the ANC's anti-apartheid guerrilla army, insisted that legislators should have an opportunity to debate every procurement plan before any money was committed.
"The next time we see these proposals will be next year and by then the decisions with respect to the 1997/98 budget will have been made. I would not want that to happen.
"It is very, very important that before the 97/98 budget is approved in any form, the committee must have an opportunity to discuss it," he said.
The defence department's presentation was based on a continuation of the current 10.7 billion rand funding level, with three billion allocated to capital projects.

Defence spending has been cut by more than half since the height of the apartheid era, when white-ruled South Africa was at war in Angola against a combined force of anti-apartheid guerrillas and the Angolan army backed by Cuba.
